summary:
The Islamic Penal Code criminalises all same-sex activity for men and women, with penalties running from flogging to the death penalty. Articles 233 to 239 define the offences in anatomical terms and set 100 lashes for the receptive partner in sodomy, 100 lashes for intercrural sex, 31 to 74 lashes for other intimate acts between men, and 100 lashes for tribadism with death on a fourth conviction; the code does not distinguish consensual from non-consensual conduct, and NGOs report that in assault cases both victim and perpetrator are held criminally liable. The UK Home Office country report (CPIN, version 5.0, December 2025) records that the code carries no discrimination protections of any kind and that convictions are frequently brought on the pretext of more severe charges. Outright International confirms that same-sex relations are illegal nationwide for both sexes.

The enforcement backdrop is documented and long-standing. Human Rights Watch recorded two men executed for homosexual conduct on 21 November 2005; an encyclopaedia compilation cites at least 107 executions on homosexuality-related charges between 1979 and 1990, a raw count with no population denominator and no per-capita basis for comparison. Raids on private gatherings recur across provinces: 87 people arrested at a birthday party in Isfahan in May 2007, 30 men arrested at a party in Isfahan in February 2008 and held without a lawyer, and an April 2017 IRGC raid on a private party in Isfahan Province in which agents fired weapons and used electric Tasers, with detainees taken to Dastgerd Prison and told they would be executed. Security forces raid houses and monitor internet sites for information on LGBTI persons, those accused of sodomy face summary trials, and 6Rang has documented forced anal or sodomy tests and degrading treatment of persons charged with homosexual conduct.

Recognition of trans status exists but is conditional and surgical. Legal-religious authorisation traces to a 1964 fatwa issued while Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini was in exile, an 1983 fatwa allowing operations as a cure for diagnosed transsexuals, and a 1985 reaffirmation, with practice legal since the mid-1980s under medical approval. The CPIN states that recognition follows only after surgery, sterilisation and a lengthy legal process; that the surgery is invasive and often carried out to sub-standard practice; and that an LGBT+ person living openly without recognised surgery is likely to face persecution. Petitioners must invoke Article 215 of the civil code on 'rational benefit' with medical approval supporting a dissonance between assigned and experienced gender.

That tolerance is coercive. Some gay people are pressured to undergo sex reassignment surgery to avoid legal and social persecution for being gay, with medical-legal endorsement framing reassignment as a route to heteronormative conformity. Business Insider describes the state funding of gender-reassignment surgery as purchased at the price of dignity, and LGBTQ Nation reported in 2025 that trans medical tourism is booming in Iran, with foreign patients seeking subsidised surgery while Iranian trans people face pressure to conform to a binary transition or face legal penalty.

Trans visibility in public space is subject to official restriction: Tehran authorities publicly warned transgender people to avoid busy areas. Custodial violence against trans detainees is documented. Ghazal Marzban, an imprisoned trans rights activist, recounted rape in an open letter from a Ministry of Intelligence detention facility.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legally recognised, and no legislation addresses discrimination or bias-motivated violence on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. The death penalty is legally available from age 18 and for murder from age 15, and documented cases involving young people include the January 2008 arrest in Sardasht of two men aged 18 and 19 on sodomy and mohārebe charges, the reported 2006 hanging of two youths in north-eastern Iran, the 2022 Maragheh case in which death sentences for 'sodomy by force' stemming from an accusation by a 16-year-old boy were commuted to life imprisonment, and the May 2021 murder of 20-year-old Ali Monfared allegedly by relatives after the military mailed him an exemption document because of his sexual orientation. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship enters this same statutory exposure.
tangentialFactors:
Religious authority on reassignment is split. Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei legally recognises gender reassignment, while Grand Ayatollah Yousef Madani Tabrizi has called it unlawful and not permissible, and several senior clerics stress that reassignment is not permissible for cross-dressers or for people engaging in same-sex behaviour. Hujjat al-Islam Kariminia has stated that Iranian society remains largely unaware of the distinction between homosexuality and transsexuality.

Social treatment differs by direction of transition. The documented position is that trans men are more visible socially and find acceptance more easily than trans women, who are often misgendered and placed in the same category as gay men.

Displacement is documented as systematic rather than incidental. A 6Rang submission to the UN Independent Expert on Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity and Expression (February 2025), 'They See Us as Criminals', surveyed 25 LGBTIQ+ people who fled Iran, 96 per cent of them from ethnic minorities, and documented persecution driving displacement; a further 6Rang submission to Iran's Universal Periodic Review at the 48th session (January to February 2025) catalogued human-rights violations against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people. Iranian transgender people flee to Türkiye to seek UNHCR asylum, and since October 2008 the Iranian Railroad for Queer Refugees and the Marjan Foundation have provided basic necessities, financial aid and private sponsorship for resettlement to Canada, amid prolonged waiting periods.

Asylum outcomes in third countries are mixed. The Netherlands stopped deporting gay men to Iran temporarily in 2006, reversing an initial March 2006 statement by Immigration Minister Rita Verdonk and confirming in October 2006 that Iranian LGBT people would not be deported; the United Kingdom drew criticism for continued deportations, with news reports documenting gay Iranians who died by suicide when faced with deportation, though the cases of Kiana Firouz and Mehdi Kazemi ended in asylum grants; UNHCR rejected a plea from an Iranian man in 2001, and Japan and Sweden rejected Iranian claims in 2005. Because the government does not allow any political party or organisation to endorse LGBTQ rights, that advocacy role has fallen to exiled groups including the Green Party of Iran, the Worker Communist Party of Iran, the Worker's Way, the Glorious Frontiers Party and the Constitutionalist Party of Iran; the Shia gay cleric Mullah Taha was forced to flee in 2016 after conducting same-sex marriages.
localsOnly:
Under Article 20, Clause 14, a person who has had sex reassignment surgery may legally change name and gender on birth certification by court order, and corrected identity documents have reportedly been issued efficiently and transparently. Petitioners also invoke Article 215 of the civil code covering acts serving a 'rational benefit', subject to medical approval; a 1976 Iranian Medical Association ruling had deemed such surgeries unethical except for intersex individuals.

Since the mid-2000s the government has provided transgender people grants of up to 45 million rials (about $1,240) and loans of up to 55 million rials (about $1,500) for gender reassignment surgery, and the Ministry of Cooperatives, Labor and Social Welfare has required health insurers to cover such surgery.

New military identity cards have listed the exemption subsection applying to gay men and transgender individuals, who are classified as having mental disorders; 6Rang warned that this disclosure identifies them and exposes them to violence and discrimination. Homosexuals, bisexuals and lesbians are banned from donating blood. No educational campaign for LGBTQ people has been permitted, although the government approved and distributed a booklet explaining condoms to high school students and ran comprehensive HIV/AIDS education by the late 1990s; HIV medication is free to all Iranian citizens and several clinics offer free testing and counselling.

Same-sex couples cannot marry or register a union, and traditional families exercise strong influence over who and when their children marry; few LGBTQ Iranians come out to family for fear of rejection, and gay couples report fear of being seen together in public. Since the 1979 Revolution the legal code forbids any sexual activity outside heterosexual marriage, and enforcement has been stricter against gay men than lesbians. No domestic protection machinery prohibits sexual-orientation or gender-identity discrimination.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory documents entry, visa or airport-screening treatment that is differential to trans or gender-nonconforming travellers into Iran. Whether Iranian authorities apply any document-marker check, targeted anatomy inspection or secondary screening to foreign trans visitors is unresolved and not sourced here.

The inventory contains no trans-specific killing or violence rate for Iran and no denominator against which one could be measured, so no comparative magnitude of trans-targeted violence can be stated. The execution and raid figures cited are raw counts covering different periods and charge types, with no population or per-capita context, and they rank nothing.

The dating of the founding religious authorisation differs across accounts: one source gives a 1964 fatwa issued in exile, an 1983 fatwa and a 1985 reaffirmation, while other accounts of the same authorisation cite 1987. This discrepancy is unresolved.

Several legal and case details here derive from encyclopaedia compilations rather than primary legal texts or court records, including the article-by-article penalty schedule, the age thresholds for the death penalty, and the individual case dates. Whether the surgical-recognition rules apply to, or are recognised for, documents issued abroad is not sourced.

Frequency of enforcement against trans people specifically, as distinct from the documented enforcement against gay men, is not established by these sources.
